          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We heard Ms. Bhagat, the learned counsel appearing for the
original petitioner, namely Rajive Raturi. Mr. Siddharth Bhatnagar,
the learned Senior Counsel appearing for the Sanket Foundation (one
of the petitioners), and Mr.  Rahul  Bajaj, the learned counsel
appearing for one of the interveners, namely Mr. Amar Jain and Ms.
Sanchita Ain for one of the petitioners.
2. We also heard Ms. Aishwarya Bhati, Mr. Vikramjit Banerjee and
Miss Archana Pathak Dave, the learned ASGs appearing for the Union
of India.
3. In the course of today's hearing, all the learned counsel
assisted us in recapitulating the basic facts that gave rise to the
original judgment rendered by this Court dated 8 th of November,
2024. We looked into one of our orders dated 11th of February, 2026,
which is quite exhaustive.
4. In pursuance of the order referred to above i.e., dated 11th of
February 2026, status report has been filed on behalf of the
Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, Ministry of
Social Justice and Empowerment in the form of an affidavit duly
affirmed by one Sri Pradeep Anirudhan, Director in the Department
of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities. The status report
highlights the developments which have taken place after February
2026. The learned ASGs brought to our notice that in so far as
Built  environment  is  concerned,  the  draft  final  gazette

--- Page 29 ---
11
notification is ready. Once the final nod is given, the Rules would
be notified and they would come into force.
5. Insofar as Information and Communication Technology (ICT) is
concerned, the matter is at the stage of draft rules. Insofar as
Assistive Technologies, services and products are concerned, the
Union has prepared the draft report. In fact, Ms. Bhati, learned
ASG clarified that the draft rules insofar as Information and
Communication Technology (ICT) have been published. Along with the
status report, the draft rules have also been annexed.
6. The learned counsel appearing for the petitioners would submit
that before the draft rules are finalized and they are published in
the  official  gazette,  their  suggestions  may  be  considered
meaningfully, so that no lacuna or any deficiency is left behind
for proper implementation of the Rules or to put it in other words,
to make the provisions of the Act more effective so as to subserve
the object of the Act. Their suggestion is that the Union should
avail the services of some experts on the subjects including some
of the petitioners.
7. We are of the view that in so far as the aforesaid is
concerned, there should not be any difficulty on the part of the
Union to ensure that the Rules are not deficient in any manner and
they subserve the object of the Act on all aspects of the matter.
We  are  informed  by  the  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
petitioners that they have already tendered their suggestions to
the various Committees constituted by the Ministry. We urge the
Union to look into the suggestions put forward by each of the
petitioners and try to understand the same. We say so because once

--- Page 30 ---
12
the Rules are finalized and are notified, later it should not
happen that some shortcomings are highlighted in the same.
8. In such circumstances referred to above, we are suggesting
this keeping in mind the larger public interest and the fact that
this is a non-adversarial litigation. Some of the learned counsel
appearing for the petitioners have yet to look into the status
report filed by the Union along with the draft Rules. We request
the learned ASGs to see that one copy each of the status report
along with the draft Rules are furnished to all the stakeholders so
that they can look into the draft Rules and respond accordingly.
Let this exercise be undertaken at the earliest.
9. Mr. Bajaj pointed out that the State Governments are obliged
to appoint Commissioners in accordance with the mandate of Section
79 of The Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016.
According to him, the State Commissioners have an important role to
play  for  better,  effective,  and  meaningful  implementation  of
various provisions of the Act. He pointed out that the following
States have yet to appoint State Commissioner:
i) Delhi, ii) Haryana, iii) Rajasthan, iv) Himachal Pradesh, v)
Karnataka, vi) Andaman and Nicobar Islands, (vii) Nagaland, viii)
Puducherry, ix) Sikkim, x) Tamil Nadu.
10. We direct all the States referred to above to ensure that the
Commissioners are appointed in accordance with Section 79 of the
RPWD Act within a period of four weeks from today. This direction
shall be strictly complied with and none of the States referred to
above should exhibit any laxity in this regard. The laxity, if any,
shall be viewed very strictly.

--- Page 31 ---
13
11.  It is needless to clarify that the State concerned shall
appoint the Commissioner with an independent charge. The State
should not appoint anyone as a Commissioner holding additional
charge. 
12. Mr. Bajaj also pointed out that there is no full-time Chief
Commissioner for persons with disabilities since 2019. It is the
Secretary in the DEPwD who is holding this post as an additional
charge. This, according to him, is in the teeth of the note to Rule
30 of the RPWD Rules 2017. As according to Mr. Bajaj, the Rule
requires any Government servant to resign from Government service
on taking charge as CCPD. The Chief Commissioner and two Additional
Commissioners have to be appointed as per the mandate of Section 74
of the RPWD Act.
13. We direct the Union to ensure that the appointments of Chief
Commissioner and two Additional Commissioners in accordance with
Section 74 of the RPWD Act are undertaken within a period of four
weeks from today. We invite the attention of the Union to Rule 30,
of the Rules which reads thus:
“ 30. Qualification for appointment of Chief
Commissioner.
- No person shall be eligible for appointment
as Chief Commissioner, unless -
(a)  he  is  a  Graduate  from  a  recognized
University: Provided that preference shall be
given to persons having recognised degree or
diploma in social work or law or management or
human rights or rehabilitation or education of
persons with disabilities;
(b) he is having experience of at least twenty-
five years in a Group "A" level post in the
Central Government or a State Government or a
public sector undertaking or a semi Government
or an autonomous body dealing with disability
related matters or social sector or as a senior

--- Page 32 ---
14
level functionary in registered national and
international voluntary organizations in the
field of disability or social development:
Provided that out of the total of twenty-five
years of experience, he should have at least
three  years of  experience in  the field  of
rehabilitation or empowerment of persons with
disabilities; and
(c) he has not attained the age of sixty years
as on 1st January of the year of recruitment.
Note. - If he is in the service under the
Central Government or a State Government, he
shall seek retirement from such service before
his appointment to the post.”
14. One another aspect of the matter on which our attention was
drawn is Section 89 of the RPWD Act. Section 89 of the Act provides
for punishment for contravention of provisions of Act or Rules or
regulations made thereunder. Section 89 reads thus:
“89. Punishment for contravention of provisions
of Act or rules or regulations made thereunder.—
Any person who contravenes any of the provisions
of this Act, or of any rule made thereunder
shall for first contravention be punishable with
fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees and
for any subsequent contravention with fine which
shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees but
which may extend to five lakh rupees.”
15. All  the  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  petitioners
submitted  that  although  the  Act  provides  for  punishment  for
contravention of the provisions of the Act or Rules or regulations,
yet there is no mechanism in so far as mode of recovery of fine is
concerned. This, according to them, should be taken care of by the
rule making process. The rules should provide a mechanism for
effective recovery of the fine by way of punishment. We impress

--- Page 33 ---
15
upon the Union to look into this aspect of the matter and see to it
while finalizing the Rules that adequate mechanism insofar as mode
of recovery of fine is concerned is appropriately provided.
16. In the last, Mr. Bajaj pointed out that compliance with
existing accessibility standards must continue unabated. He brought
to our notice the observations made by this Court in para 83 of the
main judgment, which reads thus:
“it is clarified that progressive compliance
with the standards listed in the existing Rule
15 (1) and the progress towards the targets of
the “Accessible India campaign” must continue
unabated”.
17. The issuance of the non-negotiable norms must be completed
within a period of six months from today. We hope and trust that
this entire exercise should now be completed within the aforesaid
period.
18.  Post this matter to report compliance of our directions on
20.01.2027. 
(SACHIN KUMAR SRIVASTAVA)                           (POOJA SHARMA)
   COURT MASTER (SH)                             COURT MASTER (NSH)

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. This Court by order dated 11.12.2024, after having taken note of the rival
contentions, had observed thus:
“It is clear now that the ground truthing and the demarcation
of wetland boundary is the next step, which is to be undertaken by
each  of  the  State/UT  Wetland  Authorities  in  coordination  with
concerned nodal Department as provided under the Rules. It is a
Statutory function which has been assigned to them under the
Rules.  We,  therefore,  direct  each  of  the  State/UT  Wetland
Authorities to complete ground truthing as well as the demarcation
of wetland boundaries of each of the Wetland which have been
identified for their State by Space Application Center Atlas (SAC
Atlas), 2021.
For easy accessibility of this, each of the State/UT Wetland
Authorities shall complete this work as expeditiously as possible,
but definitely within a period of three  months  from  today. Ms.
Aishwarya Bhati, learned Additional Solicitor General, has assured
8

--- Page 42 ---
this Court that they shall be doing the monitoring with each of the
State and shall file a detailed affidavit before the next date of
listing.” 
2. It is stated that some of the States had undertaken the aforesaid task and it
is yet to be completed. Mr. Jayant Bhushan and Ms.  Anitha Shenoy, learned
senior counsels appearing for the petitioners along with Ms. Rebecca George,
learned counsel, would draw the attention of the Court to the orders passed by
this Court and contend that though some of the States have undertaken the
task, it is only on paper the identification of water bodies has been carried out
but not on physical examination or, in other words, there has been no physical
checking of these wetlands which have been identified by Space Application
Center Atlas (SAC Atlas). They would also submit that on such identification, the
demarcation which has to take place, which is also not undertaken physically
and very purpose of identifying the wetlands, would be defeated if this exercise
would not be undertaken.
3. Learned counsel appearing for the Wetlands Authority for the State of Goa
would submit that the said authority would be bound by the enactment, rules
and regulations made thereunder and as such only the wetlands as described
thereunder are being identified, checked and demarcated.
4. When our order dated 11.12.2024 which has been reiterated on 19.08.2025,
07.10.2025 and 28.10.2025 is clear, we fail to understand as to how the States
or its instrumentalities or the wetlands authorities of the concerned States, can
take a different view from the one we have already expressed in our order. We
reiterate the same and clearly state that ground truthing and demarcation of
wetland boundary should not only be on paper but also to be physically carried
out and identification of such wetlands or water bodies as identified by the
Space Application Center Atlas (SAC Atlas) shall be undertaken by all the States
if not already undertaken and a report be filed before this Court expeditiously
and at any rate within an outer limit of two months. This exercise of physical
verification if not undertaken, the Secretaries of Ministry of Environment and
Forest and the Vice Chairman of the respective States, Wetland Authorities of
the respective states shall appear in person on next date of hearing and show
9

--- Page 43 ---
cause  as  to  why  further  steps  should  not  be  taken  by  this  court  for  non-
compliance of the directions issued. It is made clear that any infraction of this
order or the earlier orders passed would be viewed very seriously.
5. Having regard to voluminous records involved in these appeals we hereby
reappoint Ms. Shibani Ghosh as nodal counsel, who shall coordinate with the
respective learned advocates appearing for the parties, State Governments,
Wetland Authorities and other respondents and shall compile the pleadings etc.
The  email  id  of  Ms.  Shibani  Ghosh  is  scwetlandsmatter@gmail.com     for  the
purpose.
6.  Mr. Laxmikant Matadan Shukla seeks leave of the Court to retire from the
case on the ground that he has handed over the NOC/Vakalatnama to Mr. Arjun
Kakkar, who undertakes to file vakalatnama. In view of the same, Mr. Shukla
stands discharged.
I.A. No.76117 of 2025 
1. Heard Mr. M K Balkrishnan, party/intervener appearing in person.
2. By  this  application  the  intervener(s)  is  seeking  for  a  direction  to  the
respondent-Union  of  India  and  others  to  pay  a  sum  of  Rs.80  crores  for
undertaking the restoration of more than 1000 kunds situated in Vrindavan said
to  be  in  80%  of dilapidated condition.  Reiterating  the  same  the  intervener
appearing in person would submit these lakes or ponds or water bodies or
kunds were established by Lord Krishna himself and as such there is divinity
attached to the same and hence the said amount be released to him, so as to
undertake the renovation and restoration of the same.
3. The  object  with  which  the  said  application  has  been  filed  though  very
laudable, in a welfare State, an individual cannot be permitted to carry out work
of this nature in a public place or in a private land or through an organization,
as claimed. The water bodies in the entire country having been identified SAC
Atlas  vests  with  the  wetland  authority  of  the  State  and/or  different
instrumentalities of the State. Hence, on the basis of the report that we have
10

--- Page 44 ---
received, which has been called for by this Court in the very same petition,
appropriate directions to the State and its instrumentalities would be issued and
as such, the prayer of the intervener cannot be entertained and accordingly it
stands rejected.
4. With this observation I.A. No.76117 of 2025 stands rejected.
I.A. No. 30632 of 2025    
This application would be considered along with the main matter.
I.A. No. 103394 of 2025
1. Heard Mr. M K Balkrishnan, party/intervener, appearing in person.
2. By  this  application,  the  intervener(s)  is  seeking  for  a  direction  to  the
respondent-Union of India and others to collect the waste from the banks of holy
rivers/shores and same be used for recycling contending  inter alia  that there
are  more than 400 rivers and the banks of these rivers are filled with plastic,
inorganic chemicals and organic waste and as such there is an urgent need to
cleanse the river banks. It is causing harm to aquatic and eco-system also. It is
prayed  that  the  project  can  be  linked  with  “Swachh  Bharat  Abhiyan”  and
“Namami  Gange  Programme”  Schemes  of  the  Central  Government.  Hence,
Intervener(s) is seeking for a direction to the Union Government to pay a sum of
Rs.1,03,800 crores to the applicant to undertake said work.
3. Having heard the intervener, we notice that the intent behind the application
as well as the cause that is being espoused by the applicant is a benevolent
cause. However, it does not cloth the intervener with a right to seek for a
direction for release of the amount of Rs.1,03,800 crores to an individual more
particularly when these subjects are State subjects. This Court would definitely
take note of the contentions raised and pass appropriate suitable directions at
the time of the final order being passed, if required.
4. With this observation, the I.A.No.103394 of 2025 stands rejected.

infructuous and accordingly it stands dismissed as having become infructuous.

NON-REPORTABLE
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.              OF 2026
(ARISING OUT OF SLP (CRL.) NO.1783 OF 2026)
MOHAMMED ABDUL AHAD 
SHAKER … APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF TELANGANA AND 
ANOTHER … RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
AUGUSTINE GEORGE MASIH, J.
1. Leave granted.
2. The  present  appeal  challenges  the  judgment
and  order  dated  22.09.2025  passed  by  the
High  Court  of  Telangana  at  Hyderabad  in
Criminal Petition No.12339/2025 whereby the
High Court dismissed the petition filed by the
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.1783/2026                                          Page 1 of 10

--- Page 59 ---
appellant,  and  refused  to  quash  the
proceedings  arising  out  of  FIR  No.90/2020
dated 05.06.2020 pending trial before the VIIth
Additional  Chief  Metropolitan  Magistrate  at
Nampally, Hyderabad as C.C. No.7840/2020.
 
3. The factual  background, in brief, is that  on
05.06.2020 at about 05:00 pm, the appellant
was driving a black Honda Activa with the rear
number plate covered with a black mask. The
complainant,  being  on  patrol  duty,  stopped
and  apprehended  him.  FIR  bearing
No.90/2020  came  to  be  lodged  against  him
under  Sections  420  of  the  IPC  and  Section
80(a)  of  the  Motor  Vehicles  Act,  1988
(hereinafter,  “MV  Act”),  alleging  that  he  had
deceived  the  police  by  attempting  to  avoid
traffic challans.  Subsequently,  a chargesheet
bearing No.48/2020 was filed on 19.08.2020,
upon  which  cognizance  was  taken  by  the
Magistrate and a case came to be registered
bearing  C.C. No.7840/2020.
4. On 17.09.2025, the appellant filed a petition
under  Section  528  of  the  BNSS  bearing
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.1783/2026                                          Page 2 of 10

--- Page 60 ---
No.12339/2025 before the High Court seeking
quashing of the proceedings against him.
5. By way of the impugned judgment and order
dated  22.09.2025,  this  petition  came  to  be
dismissed, noting that the prima facie case was
made  out  and  the  appellant  could  not  have
masked  the  number  plate  under  any
circumstances.
6. Aggrieved, the appellant is now before us by
way of the present appeal.
7. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that
the High Court failed to appreciate  that  the
ingredients of the offence under Section 420 of
the IPC are not made out. The only allegation
against the appellant is that he covered the
rear  number  plate.  This  does  not  meet  the
statutory  ingredients  of  cheating.  Moreover,
had there been any intention of cheating, the
front  number  plate  would  also  have  been
covered. Therefore, even if the allegations are
taken at face value, they do not constitute any
criminal offence. The reasoning offered by the
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.1783/2026                                          Page 3 of 10

--- Page 61 ---
prosecution, that it would be difficult to trace
the  offender  in  case  some  crime  occurs,  is
merely conjectural. 
8. With regard to the offence under Section 80(a)
MV  Act,  it  is  submitted  that  although  such
provision  does  not  exist,  Rule  80-A  of  the
Telangana  Motor  Vehicles  Rules  relates  to
improper display of number plate. At most, the
general provision under Section 177 of the MV
Act may be invoked which only provides for a
penalty of Rs.500/- for the first offence, and
Rs.1,500/- for the second offence for violation
of  any  provisions  of  the  Act  or  rules
thereunder.
 
9. Learned counsel for the respondent State, on
the  other  hand,  supports  the  impugned
judgment  and  order,  contending  that  prima
facie case is made out, and prays for dismissal
of the appeal.
10. The settled position of law as laid down by this
Court  in  State of Haryana  and  Others v.
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.1783/2026                                          Page 4 of 10

--- Page 62 ---
Bhajan Lal and Others 1 is that the power of
quashing of proceedings ought to be exercised
when  the  allegations,  even  if  taken  at  face
value, do not prima facie make out any offence.
Paragraph 102 reads as hereunder:
“102. In the backdrop of the interpretation of
the  various  relevant  provisions  of  the  Code
under  Chapter  XIV  and  of  the  principles of
law enunciated by this Court in a series of
decisions  relating  to  the  exercise  of  the
extraordinary power under Article 226 or the
inherent  powers  under  Section  482  of  the
Code  which  we  have  extracted  and
reproduced  above,  we  have  given  the
following  categories  of  cases  by  way  of
illustration  wherein  such  power  could  be
exercised  either  to  prevent  abuse  of  the
process of any court or otherwise to secure the
ends of justice, though it may not be possible
to lay down any precise, clearly defined and
sufficiently  channelised  and  inflexible
guidelines or rigid formulae and  to give an
exhaustive  list  of  myriad  kinds  of  cases
wherein such power should be exercised.
(1)  Where  the  allegations  made  in  the  first
information  report  or  the  complaint,  even  if
they  are  taken  at  their  face  value  and
accepted in their entirety do not prima facie
constitute  any  offence  or  make  out  a  case
against the accused.
(2)  Where  the  allegations  in  the  first
information report and other materials, if any,
accompanying  the  FIR  do  not  disclose  a
cognizable offence, justifying an investigation
1 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.1783/2026                                          Page 5 of 10

--- Page 63 ---
by police officers under Section 156(1) of the
Code except under an order of a Magistrate
within  the  purview  of  Section  155(2)  of  the
Code.
(3)  Where  the  uncontroverted  allegations
made in the FIR or complaint and the evidence
collected  in  support  of  the  same  do  not
disclose the commission of any offence and
make out a case against the accused.
(4) Where, the allegations in the FIR do not
constitute a cognizable offence but constitute
only a non-cognizable offence, no investigation
is  permitted  by  a  police  officer  without  an
order of a Magistrate as contemplated under
Section 155(2) of the Code.
(5) Where the allegations made in the FIR or
complaint  are  so  absurd  and  inherently
improbable on the basis of which no prudent
person can ever reach a just conclusion that
there  is  sufficient  ground  for  proceeding
against the accused.
(6)  Where  there  is  an  express  legal  bar
engrafted in any of the provisions of the Code
or the concerned Act (under which a criminal
proceeding is instituted) to the institution and
continuance of the proceedings and/or where
there is a specific provision in the Code or the
concerned  Act,  providing  efficacious  redress
for the grievance of the aggrieved party.
(7) Where a criminal proceeding is manifestly
attended  with  mala  fide  and/or  where  the
proceeding  is  maliciously  instituted  with  an
ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance on the
accused and with a view to spite him due to
private and personal grudge.”
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.1783/2026                                          Page 6 of 10

--- Page 64 ---
11. Having heard learned counsel for the parties
and on perusal of the materials on record, we
are of the opinion that such prima facie offence
as pressed into service is not made out.
12. Section 420 of the IPC reads as hereunder:
“420.  Cheating  and  dishonestly  inducing
delivery of property.—
Whoever  cheats  and  thereby  dishonestly
induces  the  person  deceived  to  deliver  any
property to any person, or to make, alter or
destroy the whole or any part of a valuable
security,  or  anything  which  is  signed  or
sealed,  and  which  is  capable  of  being
converted into  a  valuable security, shall  be
punished  with  imprisonment  of  either
description for a term which may extend to
seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.”
13. From a bare perusal of the above, the essential
ingredients  to  constitute  the  offence  of
cheating are: 
(1) Dishonest intention
(2) Inducement of a person, and 
(3) Delivery  of  property,  or  alteration  or
destruction of valuable property.
14. When applied to the facts at hand, we find that
these essential ingredients are not made out.
The  only  allegation  against  the  appellant  is
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.1783/2026                                          Page 7 of 10

--- Page 65 ---
that he was travelling on his Activa scooty with
a black mask covering his rear number plate.
There is no material on record to show that
such  an  act  was  done  with  a  dishonest
intention, or that such an act induced a person
and caused any wrongful gain or loss. 
15. The mere apprehension of the police that the
rear  number  plate  was  covered  in  order  to
avoid challans, or  that  in case a crime was
committed, it would be difficult to trace out the
offender is at best, speculative.
16. We are further of the view that the selective
covering of only the rear number plate, leaving
the  front  plate  visible  and  legible,  is  itself
inconsistent with any planned scheme to evade
identification or detection, and goes against the
existence of a dishonest intention as alleged.
The  regulatory  breach  of  obstructing  the
number  plate  under  the  MV  Act  and  rules
thereunder  cannot  be  dressed as  an  offence
under  Section  420  of  the  IPC  without
establishing  the  essential  ingredients  as
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.1783/2026                                          Page 8 of 10

--- Page 66 ---
required.
17. Therefore, the allegations, even if taken at face
value do not constitute the offence of cheating
and  continuation  of  proceedings  against  the
appellant would amount to abuse of process of
law.
18. In light of the above, the judgment and order of
the  High  Court  calls  for  interference.  The
impugned order dated 22.09.2025 is set aside
and  the  proceedings  arising  out  of  FIR
No.90/2020  and  pending  before  the  VIIth
Additional  Chief  Metropolitan  Magistrate,
Nampally,  Hyderabad  as  C.C.  No.7840/2020
stand quashed.
19. We clarify that this quashing shall not affect
the  appellant’s  liability  to  pay  the  penalty
under Section 177 of the MV Act, which the
appellant  is  directed  to  deposit  before  the
concerned authority within one month, if not
already done.
 
20. The appeal is allowed in the aforesaid terms.
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.1783/2026                                          Page 9 of 10

--- Page 67 ---
21. Pending applications, if any, stand disposed of.

O R D E R
1. Permission to file special leave petition(s)
is allowed.

aside abatement, if any.
4. Application(s)  for  intervention/impleadment
is/are allowed.
1

--- Page 79 ---
5. Leave granted.
6. The appellant(s) is/are aggrieved by certain
observations  made  by  the  High  Court  while
disposing of the contempt petitions, particularly
those contained in paragraph 64 of the impugned
order. 
7. Paragraph 64 is reproduced hereinbelow :(Page
18)
“64. The present District Collector, Ranga Reddy
District,  shall  complete  the  process  of
determination of market value of the property of
the petitioner as on 01-10-2004, after giving
notice  to  petitioner's  counsel/petitioner,
consider  the  material  produced  by  the
petitioner,  and  determine  the  compensation
payable to the petitioner as per the decision in
Mekala Pandu (1 supra) and as per the law
declared  by  various  Courts  in  relation  to
acquisition of land under the Land Acquisition
Act, 1894, and pay the same to petitioner within
eight weeks.”
8. The  substantive  judgment,  alleged  non-
compliance of which give rise  to the contempt
proceedings, was passed on 20th September, 2004.
9. The operative portion of the said judgment is
reproduced hereinbelow : (Pages 102-103)
2

--- Page 80 ---
“When the matters were heard, the learned
standing  counsel  for  APIIC  Sri  R.Subba  Rao
brought to the notice of this Court that in all
the matters possession was taken by the Revenue
Department after depositing the exgratia amount
with  the  Deputy  Collector/Mandal  Revenue
Officer of Serilingampally Mandal and that when
the amount at the rate of Rs.2,00,000/- (Rupees
two lakhs only) per acre was sent by way of
cheque to the assignees, they refused to accept
the cheque, and therefore. the amount is with
the  Mandal  Revenue  Officer,  Serilingampally
Mandal.  There  is  a  dispute,  however,  with
regard to the possession of the land. Having
regard  to  the  fact  that  this  Court,  while
passing interim orders, gave liberty to the
respondents  to  take  possession  of  the  land
after depositing exgratia amount and possession
was taken by the Revenue officials under the
cover of Pachnama, there is no strong reason to
disbelieve the version of the respondents.
In L.A.O. v. M.Pandu (supra), the Full Bench of
this Court considered the question whether the
assignees  are  entitled  to  payment  of
compensation and other benefits payable under
the provisions of Land Acquisition Act, 1894
when the assigned lands are resumed by the
Government for public purpose. Answering the
question in the affirmative, this Court laid
down as under.
In  the  circumstances,  we  hold  that  the
assignees of the Government lands are entitled
to payment of compensation equivalent to the
full  market  value  of  the  land  and  other
3

--- Page 81 ---
benefits on par with full owners of the land
even in cases where the assigned lands are
taken possession of by the State in accordance
with the terms of grant or patta, though such
resumption is for a public purpose. We further
hold that even in cases where the State does
not invoke the covenant of the grant or patta
to resume the land for such public purpose and
resorts to acquisition of the land under the
provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894,
the assignees shall be entitled to compensation
as  owners  of  the  land  and  for  all  other
consequential benefits under the provisions of
the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. No condition
incorporated in patta/deed of assignment shall
operate as a clog putting any restriction on
the  right  of  the  assignee  to  claim  full
compensation as owner of the land.
Initially, all the writ petitions were filed
challenging the action of the respondents in
resuming the land without paying compensation
under  the  Executive  orders.  Even  after
amendment in some of the writ petitions, the
petitioners are interested only to receive the
compensation/exgratia equivalent to full market
value as held by the Full Bench of this Court.
Therefore, whether the possession is taken or
not insignificant, as the respondents do not
deny the legal position enunciated by the Court
in L.A.O. v. M.Pandu (supra).
In view of the settled legal position, all the
writ  petitions  are  disposed  of  directing
respondents 1 and 2, and the Government of
Andhra Pradesh to pay the compensation to all
4

--- Page 82 ---
the petitioners equivalent to full market value
of the land and other benefits on par with full
owners of the land. It is brought to the notice
of  this  Court  by  Sri  Ch.Siddaiah,  learned
counsel for the petitioners in some of the writ
petitions, that the Government had acquired the
land of the owners sometime last year. If that
be  so,  the  Government  may  also  take  into
consideration the  compensation fixed  by the
Land Acquisition Officer in those acquisition
proceedings. Respondents shall take appropriate
action  for  payment  of  market  value  to  the
petitioners, within a period of four months
from the date of receipt of a copy of this
order. The interim orders passed shall stands
vacated. It shall be open to the Government to
deal with the amount deposited by the APIIC
appropriately. No costs.”
10. The grievance of the appellant(s) is that the
Writ Court did not prescribe any cut-off date for
determining the market value, nor did it  confine
the relief to compensation in respect of  the
land alone but has specifically provided that all
benefits, at par with those granted  to the full
owners, be extended to  the  assignee(s)[the
appellant(s)]  without  any distinction.
11. However,  while  dealing  with  the  contempt
proceedings,  the   High  Court  confined  the
determination  of  the  market  value  as  on  1 st
5

--- Page 83 ---
October, 2004 and restricted the relief only to
the determination of the compensation payable to
the appellant(s).
12. It is well settled that a Contempt Court
cannot go behind the substantive judgment, nor can
it modify the same. 
13. Accordingly, we set aside the  observations
contained  in  paragraph  64  of  the  impugned
judgment/order to the extent that they restrict
the determination of the market value as on 1 st
October, 2004 and limit the relief to payment of
compensation  alone.  The  appellant(s)  shall  be
entitled to all the benefits as contained in the
judgment dated 20th September, 2004.
14. The respondents shall ensure full compliance
with the judgment dated 20th September, 2004 within
a  period  of  two  months,  failing  which  the
appellant(s) shall be at liberty to apply for
appropriate orders by approaching this Court by
way of an appropriate application in this disposed
of appeal itself.
15. The  appeals are, accordingly, disposed of.
6

--- Page 84 ---
16. In view of the order passed in the appeals
above mentioned, the contempt petition shall stand
disposed of.
17. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. This appeal is at the instance of some of the home buyers of a

--- Page 90 ---
project by name “NCR Greens” floated by the respondent No.4, namely
Siddharth Build Home Private Limited (Developer), Delhi against the
order dated 09.09.2025 passed by the NCLAT by which the Appellate
Tribunal disposed of one IA bearing No.3206 of 2025 and one Company
Appeal No.1041 of 2025 preferred by Punjab and Sind Bank came to be
dismissed. 
2. The operative part of the order passed by the NCLAT reads
thus:
“11.  Shri Sumant Batra, Learned Counsel for the
Respondent  No.4  promoter/director  supported  the
impugned order and submits that the interpretation put
by the Adjudicating Authority on Section 25A is in
accord  with the statutory scheme. It is submitted that
as per proposal under Section 12A, NCR Greens Project
and Estella Project were to be completed within six
months  and  one  year  respectively.  A  Monitoring
Committee has been constituted comprising of a Retd.
Chief  Justice  of  High  Court  and  there  are  other
members. Several meetings have been held by Monitoring
Committee and substantial progress has been made. The
project NCR Greens is almost complete. The possession
shall also be handed over till the end of February of
135 semi furnished units which shall be completed by
then. Out of 653 units in project NCR Green, 415 units
have already been handed over. It is submitted that
Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No.791 
of 2023 filed by the Resolution Professional is not
maintainable since Resolution Professional cannot be
said  to  be  an  aggrieved  person.  On  23.11.2023,
possession has issued of 103 units. As far as the
Estella  Project  is  concerned,  upon  direction  of
Monitoring Committee, the structural audit to ensure
the future safety of the families who will reside is
going on. It is submitted that the homebuyers of NCR

--- Page 91 ---
Greens are satisfied with the progress and that is why
application IA No.753 of 2023 was filed by homebuyers
of Sidhartha Buildhome Pvt. Ltd. praying that the
proposal under Section 12A should be approved. Shri
Batra further submits that the Resolution Professional
has counted the votes of each homebuyer individually,
instead of considering the decision by the majority of
class of creditors as a single vote in proportion to
their voting share percentage. Calculation of votes
individually is unsustainable. Plain reading of proviso
of Section 25A(3), it is clear that by referring to the
term 'several Financial Creditors' the legislature has
simply  referred  to  'several  classes  of  Financial
Creditors' or else, the purpose for the appointment of
the Authorised Representative would be defeated if he
had to cast his vote in respect of each homebuyer
individually, because in that case, homebuyers could
have directly casted their votes without appointing the
Authorised Representative. It is submitted that the
purpose of formation of 'class' would be defeated if
the  votes  are  to  be  counted  individually.  It  is
submitted that in view of the substantial progress
towards construction in both the projects and the fact
that Project NCR Greens is almost complete, in event it
is necessary to revive the CIRP, reverse CIRP be
directed for NCR Greens Project and Project Estella be
taken under CIRP.
12.  Counsel  for  the  parties  in  support  of  their
submissions have relied on several judgments of the
Hon'ble Supreme Court and this Tribunal which shall be
referred  to  while  considering  the  submissions  in
detail.
13. We have considered the submissions of the Counsel
for the parties and perused the record.

--- Page 92 ---
14.  The  principal  issue  which  has  come  for
consideration before us in these appeals is regarding
manner  of  computation  of  voting  with  regard  to
application under Section 12A. Section 12A application
submitted by promoter/director- Respondent No.4 was
considered in 27th CoC meeting held on 10.01.2023. E-
voting  which  was  conducted  between  14.01.2023  to
18.01.2023 and result of voting Resolution Professional
has recorded in the minutes that two proposals have not
been approved. In IA No.753 of 2023, voting result as
recorded by Resolution Professional on 12A application
was challenged and it was pleaded in the application IA
No.753 of 2023 that the proposal under Section 12A
stood approved.”
3. Our order dated 2 nd of December, 2025 is quite exhaustive, it
speaks for itself. In pursuance of our order dated 2 nd of December
2025, the NCLAT looked into the proposal put forward by the
respondent No.4 insofar as one another project by name “Estella” is
concerned. We should clarify at this stage that this appeal as such
has nothing to do in so far as project “Estella” is concerned. This
appeal has something to do with project “NCR Greens”. However, in
the course of hearing that took place over a period of time, we
were  given  to  understand  that  these  two  projects  have  some
connection.
4. Be that as it may. Now we have an order passed by the NCLAT
dated 05.05.2026. In the said order, the NCLAT has observed in para
22 as under:
“The above agreement dated 24.03.2026 filed by the
Appellant brought on record with BCD Mumbai Pvt. Ltd.
does not inspire any confidence nor any kind of
liability has been taken by BCD nor it can be said

--- Page 93 ---

Project Estella cannot be accepted. In view of the

accepted with respect to Project Estella.”
5. Thus, the plain reading of para 22 would indicate that the
proposal put forward by the respondent No.4 in so far as project
“Estella” is concerned, did not find favour with the NCLAT on
various aspects. This matter insofar “Estella” is concerned, should
come to an end, so far as this Court is concerned. If the
respondent No. 4 has anything else to say in this regard, it is
open for him to proceed further in accordance with law.
6. In so far as the project “NCR Greens” is concerned, we are
informed that 10 towers have already come up. The project is on the

Counsel appearing for the respondent No.4, almost 400 home buyers
have been put into possession. At this stage, we must also take
note of what the learned counsel appearing for the Punjab and Sind

the  Punjab  and  Sind  Bank,  the  Developer  owes  an  amount  of

--- Page 94 ---
approximately Rs.119 Crores for which CIRP proceedings have been
ordered to be initiated.
7. In the aforesaid context, our attention was drawn to paras 26
and 27 respectively of the order passed by the NCLAT dated
05.05.2026 May 2026. Paras 26 and 27 respectively read thus:
“26. The Promoter who has launched its project and
has  made  a  statement  before  this  Tribunal  on
16.02.2024  that  it  shall  handover  the  units
immediately,  was  the  reason  for  this  Tribunal

Promoter is under obligation to complete the project
as per its statement recorded in our order dated

--- Page 95 ---
Creditors which also include the Punjab & Sind Bank.

to Financial Creditors in Class and Punjab & Sind

According to the learned counsel appearing for the Punjab and Sind
Bank, for the purpose of grant of approval, the Developer needs to

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

SNEHA SHANKAR KATARIYA & ORS.      …. APPELLANT

  RESPONDENT(S)
With 
Contempt Petition (C) No.151 of 2024 
In SLP (C) No. 19677 of 2023
O R D E R
1. The claim of temporary injunction against the creation of
third-party rights on the property, was concurrently declined by
the trial court and the High Court, in first appeal. The plaintiffs
are before us seeking interim injunction. 
2. The  appellants  who  are  the  plaintiffs  filed  the  suit  for
declaration, on the strength of a sale deed dated 20.01.1994
and  prayed  for  setting  aside  a  Correction  Deed  dated
11.10.1996  and  numerous  sale  deeds  in  favour  of  various
defendants, allegedly executed subsequent to the deed, on the
strength of which the suit had been filed. It has to be observed
that the sale deed was of the year 1994 and though it is said to
have  been  produced  before  the  Registrar  immediately
thereafter,  the  same  was registered only in  the  year 2001.
Page 1 of 4

--- Page 98 ---
However, the sale deed in favour of the developer, who was
one of the defendants, was also of the year 2001, but it was
registered prior to the deed of 1994, on which the plaintiffs
raise their claim.
3. The High Court confirmed the rejection of the prayer for
injunction finding that the power of attorney said to have been
executed along with the agreement of sale on 14.07.1994 did
not figure the 17 th defendant. Defendant No.17 admittedly was
the  co-owner  of  the  subject  property  and  got  mutated  her
name in the Record of Rights pursuant to an application of
2019, after which she executed a sale deed on 10.09.2001 to
defendant No.68.
4. The  High Court directed for the production of certified
copy of the power of attorney referred to, in the sale deed
dated  20.01.1994,  which  on  production,  did  not  show
defendant No.17 as an executant. Defendant No.17 was also
not an executant of the agreement for sale dated 03.06.1991
and was merely a witness to that document. Further, in the
sale deed dated 20.01.1994, defendant No.17 was shown as
one of the executants, but a Correction Deed was executed
removing the name of the defendant No.17. In fact, one of the
Page 2 of 4

--- Page 99 ---
plaintiffs was a party to the Correction Deed and that deed is
now sought to be cancelled in the suit filed. 
5. It was also argued on behalf of the defendants that the
suit was misconceived since the sale deed of 1994 was sought
to be enforced through a suit in 2022; grossly delayed when
third-party rights were created and the sale deed was also of
suspicious origin and registered after a very long time without
any explanation offered for such delay.  
6. On a total conspectus of the above, we are not inclined to
interfere with the concurrent orders passed by the trial court
and the High Court. The developer is dealing with the property,
and his constructions have been held up, is the submission of
Sri Mukul Rohatgi, learned Senior Counsel for the respondents.
Sri Shyam Divan, learned Senior Counsel for the appellants,
however, submits that no third-party rights be created and if it
is so created, they be informed of the pendency of the suit.
7. On anxious consideration, we are not inclined to grant
any  order of  injunction,  restraining  alienation  or creation  of
third-party  rights,  since  this  would  amount  to  literally
frustrating  the  development  activities  in  the  property  and
Page 3 of 4

--- Page 100 ---
unsuspecting purchasers cannot be mulcted with any liability. If
the claim of the plaintiffs is upheld eventually and third-party
rights are created in the meanwhile, rather than resumption or
recovery of possession, the trial court could think in terms of
monetary  compensation  which  would  be  the  liability  of  the
developer and not the purchasers. 
8. We make it clear that the findings herein are on a prima
facie  consideration and are not intended to regulate the final
adjudication  in  the  suit.  The  rejection  of  the  prayer  for
injunction is on a finding that the prima facie case, the balance
of convenience and the irreparable injury are all in favour of
the defendants and not the plaintiffs. 
9. The civil appeal stands rejected. On the reasoning above
the contempt case also stands closed.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

Non-Reportable
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Civil Appeal No.                of 2026
[ @ Special Leave Petition (C) No.12895 of 2025 ]
Gowtham Sampath & Anr.
Through Power of Attorney
….Appellants 
Versus
Gurdeep Singh Sandhu
….Respondent
O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. The appellants who were assigned the rights with
respect to a sale agreement and who obtained a decree
for  specific  performance  based  on  it,  are  before  us
challenging the order of the High Court, condoning the
delay of 1544 days in filing an application under Order IX
Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC), as
also  the  order  setting  aside  the  ex-parte decree  and
directing disposal of the suit on its own merits. 
3. Learned Counsel appearing for the appellants relied
on the judgment in  Bhagmal and Ors. v. Kunwar Lal
and Ors. 1 wherein this Court in a similar circumstance,
on  a  challenge  against  the  rejection  of  the  prayer  for
delay condonation, allowed it and set aside the ex parte
decree itself. 
1  (2010) 12 SCC 159
Page 1 of 5
CA @ SLP(C) No.12895 of 2025

--- Page 105 ---
4. The learned Counsel appearing for the respondent,
however,  relied  on  C.  Prabhakar  Rao  and  Anr.  v.
Sama Mahipal Reddy and Anr. 2 wherein the order of
the High Court, setting aside an  ex-parte decree, when
the  application  before  it  was  only  concerned  with  the
rejection of the delay condonation, was frowned upon. 
5. We have looked at both the decisions.  Bhagmal1
was  a  case  in  which  the  trial  court  had  permitted
evidence to be led in support of the application under
Order  IX  Rule  13  CPC.  In  all,  nine  witnesses  were
examined and a compromise was projected, as arrived at
during the pendency of the suit, which was the reason for
non-appearance. The trial court rubbished the theory of
compromise as an explanation for the delay occasioned.
The trial court also rejected the application for reason of a
proper application for condonation of delay, having not
been filed; which was in the context of the contention
that the application  was  filed  within  30 days of  being
aware  of  the  ex  parte decree.  This  Court  allowed  the
appeal  accepting  the  ground  that  the  defendant  had
knowledge of the  ex-parte decree far later to it being
passed and set aside the ex-parte decree itself. The facts
are quite distinct, since that was a case in which evidence
was led in support of the Order IX Rule 13 application
which was looked into by this Court, to justify the order in
2  2025 SCC OnLine SC 495
Page 2 of 5
CA @ SLP(C) No.12895 of 2025

--- Page 106 ---
first appeal, setting aside the ex-parte decree. This has no
application to the facts of the present case.
6. In  the  present  case,  the  decree  was  passed  on
17.04.2008 as against the father of the present applicant.
The  present  applicant  contended  that  his  father  had
shifted to Muscat, where the applicant was employed, due
to old age and illness and passed away on 29.12.2009.
The appellant continued in Muscat and when he came to
India, after obtaining a release deed from the co-owners,
he visited the property in 2012 when he was made aware
of the  ex-parte  decree. There was also a ground taken
that no summons was issued to the defendant and a mere
paper  publication  was  made,  that  too,  in  a  regional
language newspaper. The High Court specifically opined
the factual aspect as to whether summons was served
properly or not, having not looked into at all, by the trial
court. If that was so, the High Court ought to have left the
decision to set aside the ex-parte decree to the trial court
and not preempted  such decision, especially when the
challenge before it was only regarding the rejection of
condonation of delay. 
7. We  are  of  the  opinion  that  C.  Prabhakar  Rao2
applies  squarely.  Therein  also  the  High  Court  in  its
revisional jurisdiction concluded that delay in filing the
Page 3 of 5
CA @ SLP(C) No.12895 of 2025

--- Page 107 ---
application to set aside the  ex-parte decree should be
condoned.  That  having  been  done,  the  Court
automatically proceeded to restore the suit and directed
the trial court to dispose of the suit expeditiously. It was
found that there was no consideration as to whether there
was a case for setting aside the ex-parte decree. 
8. On similar reasoning, we find in the present case
that  the  delay  occasioned,  having  been  properly
explained, should be condoned and we affirm the order of
the High Court to that extent. However, with respect to
the consideration of the prayer for setting aside the  ex-
parte decree, we direct the trial court to  consider the
same on its own merits. The parties shall appear before
the trial court on 17.08.2026 on which day or any near
date, evidence shall be led; the matter shall be heard, if
necessary,  the  records  perused  and  after  affording  an
opportunity of hearing to the parties, the issue decided
expeditiously. 
9. The appeal stands allowed.  
10. Pending applications, if any, shall stand disposed of.

I.A. No.147147/2018:
1. We  have  heard  Ms.  Uttara  Babbar,  learned  senior  counsel  for  the
applicant, Mr. Pitambar Acharya, learned Advocate General for the State of
Odisha  and  Mr.  Gautam  Narayan,  learned  senior  counsel  appearing  as  the
amicus curiae.
2. Our  attention  has  been drawn  to  the  order  dated  31st October,  2018
passed by a three-Judge Bench refusing the applicant’s prayer for realization of
the outstanding amount with interest @ 12% per annum. The order directed
payment of interest @ 24% per annum.
3.  It is not in dispute that subsequent to such order, payment has duly been
made by the applicant and such fact is also admitted by the State of Odisha in
paragraph 10 of the reply affidavit dated 13th January, 2026. 
4. Insofar as termination of lease for Khurigaon Manganese Mines in District
Rayagada, Odisha is concerned, we find the State of Odisha having raised an
objection that a revision is available under Section 30 of the Mines and Minerals
(Development and Regulation) Act, 1957.
5. Ms. Babbar submits that since I.A. No.147147 of 2018 has been pending
for the last eight years, any revision that may be filed now is likely to be
6

--- Page 117 ---
dismissed as time-barred. 
6. Having  heard  the  parties  and  the  learned  amicus,  we  dispose  of  I.A.
No.147147 of 2018 by observing that in the event the applicant applies for a
revision within 30 days from date, the revisional authority shall proceed to
decide the same on its own merits without limitation creating a bar. 
M.A. No.18/2025 & M.A. No.292/2025

                          RESPONDENT(s)
O R D E R
Heard learned counsel for the parties. 
2. Leave granted.
3. The present appeal basically arises out of a case under

--- Page 119 ---
2
Section  138  of  the  Negotiable  Instruments  Act,  1881
(hereinafter referred to as the “N.I. Act”) alleging dishonour
of the cheque issued by the appellant in favour of Late Shri
Hira Lal (complainant) represented by the respondents for Rs.
6,50,000/- (Rupees Six Lakhs Fifty Thousand) which, upon trial
resulted in conviction of the appellant and sentence awarded
was Simple Imprisonment for two months and compensation of Rs.
8,00,000/- (Rupees Eight Lakhs). During the pendency of the
proceedings,  the  appellant  was  granted  exemption  from
surrendering vide order dated 04.02.2026 passed by this Court.
4. Learned counsels for the parties have submitted that the
parties have entered into a compromise and the appellant has
paid the respondents a sum of Rs. 7,30,000/- (Rupees Seven
Lakhs Thirty Thousand), out of which Rs. 4,00,000/- (Rupees
Four Lakhs) has been deposited in the Trial Court and Rs.
3,30,000/-  (Rupees  Three  Lakhs  Thirty  Thousand)  has  been
transferred into the bank account of the respondents. Such fact
is not disputed by learned counsel for the respondents. 
5. For reasons aforesaid and also taking into account the fact
that the parties have compromised, vide compromise deed dated
29.01.2026, and the offence being compoundable in terms of
Section 147 of the N.I. Act, the Complaint Case bearing No. 269

--- Page 120 ---
3
of 2019(2015), filed by Late Shri Hari Lal represented by the
respondents  against  the  appellant  stands  compounded.  The
conviction and sentence of the appellant in the said case is
set aside. 
6. The appeal is allowed in the aforementioned terms.
7. We indicate that in case any impediment is caused by
appellant  in  realisation  of  the  aforesaid  compromise,  the
present  order  shall  automatically  stand  vacated  and
consequences shall ensue for the appellant.
8. After  the  order  was  passed,  learned  counsel  for  the
respondents submitted that Rs. 4,00,000/- (Rupees Four Lakhs)
which were deposited in the Trial Court by the appellant be
permitted to be withdrawn by the respondents. 
9. Accordingly, the Trial Court is directed to release Rs.
4,00,000/- (Rupees Four Lakhs) deposited by the appellant in
favour of the respondent No.1 on behalf of all respondents upon
due verification. 
10. The appeal stands disposed of in aforementioned terms.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S). 9692-9693/2024
DEPUTY DIRECTOR, DIRECTORATE OF ENFORCEMENT        APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
SHIV CHARAN & ORS.                                 RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
 By consent of the parties, the following order is passed:-
The instant civil appeal has been filed by the Directorate of
Enforcement challenging common judgment and order of the Bombay
High Court dated 01.03.2024 in Writ Petition (L) No. 9943 of 2023
and Writ Petition (L) No. 29111 of 2023.
The parties are ad idem on the proposition that the objective
of Section 8(8) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002
(for short, ‘the PMLA’) is to ultimately restore any attached
properties to bonafide claimants who have a legitimate interest in
the property attached. Considering the aforesaid position and in
the spirit of Section 8(8) of the PMLA, the Directorate of
Enforcement has, on earlier occasions, consented to the restoration
of attached properties to a Successful Resolution Applicant under
the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (hereinafter referred to
as ‘the IBC’) in (i) order dated 11.12.2024 passed by this Court in
Directorate of Enforcement vs. JSW Steel Ltd. & Ors. (C.A. No.
3362/2020), (ii) order dated 10.10.2025 passed by this Court in

--- Page 131 ---
2
SLP(C)  No.  26154-26155/2025  being  Udaipur  Entertainment  World
Private Limited vs. Union of India & Ors., and (iii) order dated
11.11.2025 passed by this Court in Criminal Appeal No. 2925/2025
being Directorate of Enforcement vs. V. Hotels Limited & Ors.
 The context of the present case is also similar. Respondent
Nos. 1-3 are the Successful Resolution Applicants (in short,
‘SRA’), in terms of the order dated 17.02.2023 passed by the
National Company Law Tribunal. The parties, in the instant appeal,
have come to a similar settlement in order to resolve the present
appeal by consent.
The attached properties, being bank balances (amounting to
Rs.3.55 lakhs) and fourteen flats/residential units (approximately
worth Rs. 32.47 crores), belonging to the Corporate Debtor i.e.
M/s. DSK Southern Projects Pvt. Ltd. covered under the Resolution
Plan are directed to be restored to the SRA, who stepped into the
shoes of the Corporate Debtor, upon successful resolution through
the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process.
This order is being passed without going into the merits and
the  rival  contentions  of  the  parties,  with  regard  to  the
correctness or otherwise of the impugned Judgment of the Bombay
High Court, and all questions of law emanating from the same are
kept open.
The present restitution order is deemed to have been passed in
terms of the second proviso to sub-Section (8) of Section 8 of
PMLA.
In view of Section 32A of the IBC, the name of the Corporate
Debtor  shall  be  deleted  from  the  array  of  accused  in  the

--- Page 132 ---
3
Prosecution Complaint bearing No.1123 of 2020 dated 03.08.2020
before the Special PMLA Court, Mumbai, while continuing with the
prosecution of the erstwhile directors and/or persons in control or
conspirators  or  abettors  and  confiscation  of  their
attached/restrained properties/entitlements, if any.
Needless to state, the benefit of Section 32A of the IBC
is subject to the condition that the SRA is neither connected with
the erstwhile Directors of the Corporate Debtor nor is the SRA a
beneficiary of proceeds of crime derived from the alleged scheduled
offence. If this foundation is eroded in the ongoing investigation,
the  Directorate  of  Enforcement  shall  be  at  liberty  to  take
appropriate steps in accordance with law, including by way of
questioning the resolution plan.
In view of the above, any challenge of the Directorate of
Enforcement to the approval of the Resolution Plan by the National
Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai, shall stand closed, and accordingly
the Directorate of Enforcement shall have no right or lien either
on  the  properties  of  the  Corporate  Debtor  attached  under
Provisional Attachment Order (PAO) No. 01/2019 dated 14.02.2019 (as
confirmed  by  the  PMLA  Adjudicating  Authority,  New  Delhi  on
05.08.2019), or on any other assets of the Corporate Debtor that
form part of the resolution plan approved by the NCLT. The
Resolution  Plan  already  stands  substantially  implemented  in
accordance with law. The attached properties shall be released by
the appellant within a period of two weeks from the date of receipt
of a copy of this order.
This order is being passed based on the peculiar facts and

--- Page 133 ---
4
circumstances of the case and with the consent of the parties under
the second proviso to sub-Section (8) of Section 8 of the PMLA, and
shall not be treated as a precedent. We once again make it clear
that the questions of law shall remain open to be decided in an
appropriate case.
We place on record our appreciation for the earnest efforts
made by the officers of the Directorate of Enforcement in restoring
the attached properties to secure the interests of justice.
We  also  reiterate  that  the  ECIR  against  the  erstwhile
directors and promoters would continue and, thus, the present order
will have no bearing on those proceedings. 
IA No.233297/2024 seeking intervention stands disposed of,
while giving liberty to place this order before the Special Court
for getting appropriate orders.
Accordingly, the appeals stand disposed of.
Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

Leave granted.
The appellant seeks bail in connection with
FIR No.6 of 2023 dated 17.02.2023, registered at
Police  Station:  EOW,  Odisha,  Bhubaneshwar,
District- Khordha, for the offences punishable
under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471 and 120B of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860; Sections 4,5 and 6 of the
Prize  Chits  and  Money  Circulation  Schemes
(Banning) Act, 1978 ;  Section 6 of the Odisha
Protection  of  Interests  of  Depositors  (in
Financial Establishments) Act, 2011, and Se ction
66(D) of the Information Technology Act, 2000.

--- Page 137 ---
2
We have heard the learned counsel appearing
for the parties.
The  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
appellant submits that apart from the period of
incarceration undergone by the appellant, there is
a delay in trial as only 30 out of 103 witnesses
have been examined.  Further, the appellant is a
fourth standard drop out, and he has been made a
scapegoat in the present case.
The  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
respondent,  by  refuting  the  said  submissions,
submits  that  considering  the  nature  of
allegations, there is no need for an interference
with the impugned order.
Suffice it is to state that the appellant has
been  under  incarceration  for  more  than  three
years, and the trial is moving at a snail’s pace.
The specific case against the appellant is that he
is the director of a company to which a sum of
Rs.11.13  crores  of  the  tainted  money  was
transferred. In other words, the appellant has

--- Page 138 ---
3
acted in collusion with the prime accused.
Considering  the  specific  case  of  the
prosecution,  coupled  with  the  period  of
incarceration already undergone by the appellant,
we are inclined to grant bail to the appellant.
However, we make it clear that this order
will not enure to the benefit of accused No.1, who
is the main accused.  If a bail application is
preferred by him in the future, the same shall be
decided on its own merits, and no parity can be
claimed.
Furthermore, the Trial Court shall impose
adequate conditions by taking note of the fact
that the appellant before us is a resident of
Rajasthan, and therefore, he should be made to
extend his continued cooperation in the conduct of
the trial, which is going on in Odisha.
Accordingly, the impugned order is set aside,
and the appellant is granted bail on such terms
and  conditions  to  the  satisfaction  of  the
concerned Trial Court.

--- Page 139 ---
4
The appeal stands allowed, accordingly.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

Non-Reportable
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Civil Appeal No.                of 2026
[ @ Special Leave Petition (C) No.943 of 2022 ]
Thattayil Orippurarth
Bhagavathy Devaswom & Ors.
….Appellants 
Versus
Gopalakrishnan & Ors.
….Respondent
O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. There has been a concerted attempt to unseat the
administrators of the first appellant temple,  which  has
been resisted stoutly by the appellants. There are various
proceedings initiated by different persons, which we need
not go into here, since we are only concerned with the
condonation of delay allowed by the High Court, by the
impugned order in a Regular First Appeal.
3. We heard Sri Gagan Gupta, learned Senior Counsel
appearing  for  the  appellants  and  Sri  V.  Chitambaresh,
learned Senior Counsel appearing for the respondents.
4. A scheme suit was filed numbered as OS No.132 of
1997, which was dismissed by an elaborate judgment as
seen from Annexure P1. The Subordinate Judge found that
there is no reason to settle a scheme, since there was
proper administration of the temple and also noticed the
contention of the contesting defendants that there was an
Page 1 of 5
CA @ SLP(C) No.943 of 2022

--- Page 155 ---
earlier  suit  filed  in  which  the  very  same  prayer  was
sought, which suit was later abandoned.
5. As we noticed, there were other proceedings also
which too turned futile. With a delay of 1381 days, some
of the plaintiffs filed an RFA in which the impugned order
was passed. The affidavit accompanied the application for
condonation of 1381 days delay only speaks of several
discussions having been carried out after the suit was
dismissed  to  settle  the  matter  amicably.  We  cannot
comprehend, why discussions should be carried out after
the suit for settlement of a scheme was dismissed. In any
event,  there is  no  cause  for  the  administrators of  the
temple to participate in any such discussions. The mere
fact of discussions having been proceeded with amongst
the  people  who  were  contesting  the  claim  of  the
administrators, cannot be a  valid  reason  for the delay
occasioned, that too of 1381 days.
6. We also have to notice that the learned Single Judge
after noticing that there is no sufficient reason to condone
the delay, purportedly to advance justice, a liberal view
was  taken.  In  fact,  we  are  of  the  opinion  that  such
proceedings to disrupt a valid administration would only
serve in advancing injustice. We hence are of the opinion
that  the  impugned  order  was  not  in  advancement  of
justice and  would only  visit the appellants with  undue
hardship and prejudice the temple itself.
7. We, hence, reverse the order of the learned Single
Judge and find the delay to be unexplained. T he appeal
stands allowed.

CA @ SLP(C) No.943 of 2022

8.  Pending applications, if any, shall stand disposed of.

       UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Vide our order dated 03 rd June, 2026, the cut-off date was
fixed as 27 th May, 2026.  It is seen that now even those
candidates who had never approached the Court, in whatever
capacity, have filed applications seeking benefit of our order
dated 03rd June, 2026.  Well this is neither permissible nor was
it the intent and spirit of our order.  As such, all such
applications shall stand dismissed.
2. Registry is directed not to entertain any such application
in future, without leave of the Court. 
3. From the affidavit dated 17 th July, 2026 filed by respondent
no.2 (Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission), it is evident that
now  the  Director  General  and  Inspector  General  of  Police,
Jharkhand has initiated the process for conducting the physical
fitness  test  of  those  candidates  who  had  cleared  their
examination and were before the Court (High Court or this Court),
in whatever capacity i.e. petitioner, appellant, respondent,
applicant, non-applicant. We direct that the whole exercise be
got completed within three weeks. Needless to add, physical
examination has to be conducted on the lines discussed during the
4

--- Page 168 ---
course of the hearing.
4. It is pointed out that some of those candidates, who had in
fact cleared their entrance examination and were parties to
proceedings in the Court(s), their names are not in the list
prepared by the Authorities.  Well as a last and final chance,
with no further extension, we direct that all candidates who may
be interested shall positively, within next two working days,
furnish their particulars along with all proof of they being
party in any one of the litigations pertaining to the process of
selection and appointment, subject matter of the present  lis,
such particulars to be furnished to the learned counsel for the
State or the Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission.  We clarify
that in default under no circumstances their cases shall be
entertained in future.
5. Mr. P.S.Patwalia, learned senior counsel, who appears on
behalf of those candidates who are serving as Home Guards and
could not clear their written examination; other learned counsel,
whose  clients  are  similarly  situate,  may  submit  their
supplementary affidavit in support of their case(s), positively
within three days.  Advance copy of such affidavit be supplied to
the other parties.  Reply thereto, if any, be filed within one
week thereafter.
6. List on 11.08.2026.

353(2),  352  and  238  of  the  Bharatiya  Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023 and Sections 66(D) and 67 of the
Information Technology Act, 2000.
We have heard the learned counsel appearing
for the parties.

--- Page 175 ---
2
The case against the appellant is that he
procured,  morphed  and  circulated  some  videos
damaging the reputation of the functionaries of a
certain political party. The complaint has been
registered at the instance of a Member of the
Legislative Assembly.
Admittedly,  the  investigation  qua the
appellant stands concluded. Even if there is a
need  for  any  continued  investigation,  the
custodial interrogation of the appellant is not
required, as we are dealing with a case involving
documentary evidence.
Suffice it is to state that the appellant is
certainly  entitled  to  the  grant  of  bail,
especially when he has been under incarceration
for seven months.

to grant bail to the appellant.

O R D E R
We have heard Ms.  Mona K. Rajvanshi, learned
counsel for the petitioner and Mr. Rahul Kaushik, learned
Senior Counsel for the respondent. The petitioner and the
respondent are present in Court, duly identified by their
respective counsel.
2. The matter relates to the custody of the minor girl
child aged about eight years, who is the daughter of
petitioner’s daughter and respondent is the biological
father of the child. There is an elder sibling of the girl
child,  aged  ten  years,  who  is  residing  with  the
respondent-father, who has re-married in the year 2019. It
transpires from the orders on record that the child wants
to live with her elder sister, as also the father.
However, it is equally true that the child is attached to
the petitioner, being his maternal grandfather and also to
1

--- Page 180 ---
the maternal side of her family.
3. On the first call, the Court requested the parties to
talk to each other and work out an amicable settlement in
the best interest of the child and also taking into
account  the  fact  that  the  petitioner  lives  in
Muzaffarnagar,  whereas  the  respondent  resides  in
Ghaziabad, which has a running distance by car of two
hours.
4. On the second call, we have been informed that the
parties have arrived at a “settlement”. The petitioner is
ready to part with the custody of the girl child and the
respondent has informed that he has already approached a
good school for getting the child admitted, which is to be
done before the middle of August, 2026. It has further
been agreed that the respondent shall go to the house of
the petitioner this Sunday, i.e., 26 th July, 2026 at 11.00
a.m. and then take the child with him. The petitioner and
his side of the family shall have full access to the
child, as also the elder sibling of the child at the house
of the respondent, and as may be agreed, both the children
can  also  visit  the  petitioner  so  that  a  cordial
relationship is not only maintained, but the bonds are
strengthened. We are confident, on the basis of what we
have been told by the parties in Court, that they will
mutually respect each other and shall not do anything
which may traumatize and cause any impediment in both the
2

--- Page 181 ---
siblings living peacefully with the father. It has also
been indicated that during the time of vacations, there
may be more accessibility and the parties may consider the
two sisters spending a few days also with the petitioner
and the maternal side.
5. It goes without saying that in today’s world, the
accessibility through mobile phone would be the first
point of access and the petitioner shall be entitled to
get details of the phone numbers of both the girls or
either  of  the  respondent-father  or  any  other  person
related to them, on which the petitioner can talk to the
two siblings.
6. The Special Leave Petitions stand  disposed of and all
earlier orders passed by the Courts stand modified by the
present order.

of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
EXTRA-ORDINARY APPELLATE JURISDICTION
PETITION FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (CIVIL) NO.15585/2023
ANAMIKA MISHRA & ORS.                           PETITIONERS
                                VERSUS
KALIPAD JANA & ORS.                             RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. The present Special Leave Petition arises out of the
impugned order dated 18.04.2023 passed by the High Court of
Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur in Miscellaneous Appeal No.2663
of 2011.
2. The facts of the case reveal that the claim petition
was preferred before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal,
Shahdol, in Claim Case No.41/2009, and the Claims Tribunal
allowed the claim in the matter. The claimants have filed an
appeal before the High Court for enhancement of compensation
and a cross objection was also preferred by the Insurance
Company. The matter has been finally remanded back to the
Claims Tribunal. The facts further reveal that, at the
relevant point of time when the claim petition was decided
by the Claims Tribunal, the insurance policy was not brought
on record, and in those circumstances, an application was
preferred under Order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil
Procedure,  1908  (for  short,  'CPC'),  for  production  of
additional  evidence  before  the  Appellate  Court.  The
PETITION FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (CIVIL)  NO.15585/2023

--- Page 185 ---
2
Appellate Court remanded the matter back to the Tribunal
after taking on record the additional evidence filed along
with the application preferred under Order 41 Rule 27 of the
CPC. The High Court also directed the Claims Tribunal to
record evidence with regard to the insurance policy and
thereafter ascertain the liability of the Insurance Company.
At this stage, it was brought to the notice of this Court by
the Insurance Company that the owner had not been impleaded
as one of the respondents before the Claims Tribunal, and
the owner is certainly a necessary party where a claim
petition is preferred.
3. The facts of the case reveal that after the award was
passed by the MACT on 03.01.2011, a Review Petition was
preferred  by  the  Insurance  Company  on  02.02.2011.  An
application under Order 6 Rule 17 of CPC was also preferred
for amendment of the written statement. However, both were
dismissed by the Claims Tribunal.
4. In the considered opinion of this Court, the High
Court has rightly remanded the matter back to the Tribunal
to record evidence with regard to the insurance policy and
to  ascertain  the  liability  of  the  Insurance  Company.
Therefore, in case the Claims Tribunal arrives at the
conclusion that the Insurance Company is not liable to pay
the claim, the Tribunal shall apply the principle of "pay
and recover" in the facts and circumstances of the case.
PETITION FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (CIVIL)  NO.15585/2023

--- Page 186 ---
3
5. Learned counsel for the petitioners has stated before
this Court that the petitioners do not have the address of
the owner. Therefore, the Insurance Company shall furnish
the details of the owner to the petitioners before the
Claims Tribunal, thereby enabling the claimants to implead
the owner as one of the respondents.
6. As it is a very old matter, the Tribunal, after
recording the evidence with regard to the insurance policy
and after hearing the owner, shall also decide the matter as
expeditiously as possible, preferably within a period of
three months. In case any appeal is preferred in the matter,
the  High  Court  is  also  requested  to  decide  it  as
expeditiously as possible at an early date, as the claim
petition is of the year 2009. The parties shall appear
before the Claims Tribunal on 10th August, 2026.
7. The Special Leave Petition stands disposed of with the
above observations and directions.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
